note: The human half of the naming gate. scripts/validate-naming.mjs checks the six mechanical rules; this records a practitioner's judgement on the rule that cannot be mechanised -- whether the name is what someone would say to ask for the operation. Review docs/widget-names.md, which is generated, and record verdicts here. A verdict is pinned to the digest of (nodeType, title, group): change any of the three and the review goes stale rather than carrying over.
ceilingRule: pendingCeiling may be lowered freely. It may be raised only when a widget is added whose FUNCTION DID NOT EXIST BEFORE -- the practitioner's rule, 2026-10-25: "we can add a widget if its function did not exist before" -- with an entry in ceilingRaises naming the widget and what it does that nothing did. That is D2 of the admission audit asked of the ceiling: a widget duplicating an existing function must not buy itself room by raising this, and a widget carrying a function the framework lacked is not review debt incurred carelessly. The ratchet exists so review debt cannot grow SILENTLY, not so that nothing may be added. As first written this rule said 'never raised' and also that the pending list 'can only shrink', which cannot both hold: a widget added after 2026-10-13 has no entry, fails the build until one is written, and a written entry starts pending. The contradiction surfaced on 2026-10-25, when rate_ratio was the second widget added in one day and the first to find no slack left.

verdicts.accepted: The name is what a practitioner would say to ask for this operation.
verdicts.flagged: Raised in review; carries a note and appears in every build until resolved.
verdicts.pending: Not yet reviewed. Seeded for the widgets that existed when this gate was added.

reviews.title: Aggregate points to H3 cells
reviews.note: Renamed from `hex_aggregate` on 2026-10-19, as the sibling of the above: same operation, different areal unit, and it had the verb after its object with the unit unstated. The unit is the ontology's own term (`fw:HexCell`, "H3 cell") rather than "hexbin", because a plotting library's hexbin is a lattice fitted to its data and these cells come from a fixed global index at a stated resolution. Hexbin is what practitioners say, so it is a glossary pointer to H3 cell and sits in the widget's description, which is what the palette search matches.

reviews.title: Total within groups
reviews.note: Epi Info's command is GROUP, but "group" alone does not say that the values are added up, and this widget offers only a sum because summing a rate is meaningless. "Total within groups" says the operation and leaves the grouping implicit in the columns kept. For review: whether a practitioner would look under "total", "sum", "aggregate" or "group".

reviews.title: Join a table to the study area
reviews.note: Pending because the practitioner named the tension while the widget was being designed, 2026-10-25: "We are not strictly joining table to polygon here. What we are joining are a table and another table with geometry." The title says "to the study area", which is the object a practitioner points at, and the identifier says `area`, which is the port. Neither says that the area carries a table of named parts and that the join is table-to-table on those names. Whether that matters to a reader is the question a review has to answer; it is not settled by the author who chose the name.

reviews.title: Relate a column from another table
reviews.note: Epi Info's own word, kept deliberately: RELATE is one of its three join commands and the one this matches, while MERGE and MATCH do different things. The tension for review is that a practitioner asking for this would probably say "join" -- and `join_table_to_area` already uses that word for putting a value onto a boundary, which is a different operation. The title is long and says what the row count does not do.

reviews.title: Select rows by value
reviews.note: Renamed from `keep_rows` on 2026-10-26 at the practitioner's verdict -- "keep_rows is not intuitive". SELECT is the command epidemiologists already know for choosing a subset before analysis, so the name needs no translation; `keep_rows` named the mechanics, and `rows` is the kind of category noun this ledger's rule rejects. Renamed before release, so no saved workflow carried the old identifier.

reviews.title: Summarize points to polygons
reviews.note: Renamed from `summarize_polygons` on 2026-10-19 after the practitioner asked whether it should be "summarize points or summarize polygons". Neither alone: the operation reduces POINTS and the polygons are the areal units it reduces them to, so both operands are named and the second carries a preposition. `summarize_combined_area` is the widget that genuinely summarizes polygons. The mechanical gate recorded no violation for the old name, which is why this ledger exists.

reviews.title: Two-by-two table
reviews.note: The name the discipline uses, and the one an FETP-trained reader will search for. For review: whether the title should also carry what it computes -- a reader looking for "risk ratio" or "odds ratio" will not find those words in the title, only in the description, which is what the palette search matches. Against that, naming one estimate in the title would make the other two look secondary.

rule: After a transform verb the slot names what the verb acts ON. A second operand is stated with a preposition -- summarize_points_to_polygon, aggregate_points_to_h3_cell, snap_to_network -- never left to the reader and never put in the object slot. A method name stands in for the operation only where the method name IS the practitioner's term, which is the existing exemption that keeps `voronoi`, `isochrone` and `summarize_hull`. Recorded 2026-10-19 with the first two reviews; see docs/audits/ontology-audit.md for the convention it corrects.

ceilingRaises.functionThatDidNotExist: Dividing one rate by another, with an interval. src/rate.ts computed one group's measure and stopped; nothing in the framework compared two measures to each other. slr_threshold_comparison compares a value to a threshold, which is not the same operation. So the framework could map Snow's mortality rates and could not state his argument.
ceilingRaises.why: The ceiling had exactly one place left and join_table_to_area took it earlier the same day. Nothing about rate_ratio's name was reviewed to make room: the debt genuinely rose by one, and is recorded rather than absorbed. Lowering it again means reviewing a pending name, which is a practitioner's judgement and not an author's.

ceilingRaises.functionThatDidNotExist: Arithmetic over a table, and selection of its rows. Rules conclude a TERM about a record and never a number computed from other numbers -- authoredProjection says so in place, "the value field is untouched" -- so no step could compute one value from two others. Nothing selected rows of a table either: clip_points_to_area filters points by geometry, and no equivalent existed for a table. The 0.12.0 release notes record the cost as a validation limit: South London's contingency table is prepared outside the application because nothing derives a column from others.
ceilingRaises.why: Two widgets, two places. Raised rather than absorbed, because absorbing it would mean recording a practitioner's verdict on a name nobody has reviewed. Both entries are pending and the ceiling carries the debt until they are read.

ceilingRaises.functionThatDidNotExist: Joining two tables, totalling a table within groups, and the analysis under a two-by-two. Nothing joined two tables on a shared column: the 0.12.0 release notes record that as the reason South London's contingency table is prepared outside the application, and `join_table_to_area` puts a value onto a boundary rather than onto rows. Nothing totalled a table either -- `rate` groups and sums internally and emits a RATE, so the totals are consumed on the way out and no other step can use them. And nothing computed a risk, a risk ratio, an odds ratio or a risk difference: the application drew a 2x2 with counts and margins and no analysis, while the only ratio on the canvas was a RATE ratio, a different estimand.
ceilingRaises.why: Three widgets, three places. Raised rather than absorbed, because lowering the ceiling means a practitioner reviewing a pending name and that is not an author's to do. The practitioner's own answer to the budget question the same day: "I am not worried about increasing the widgets because I see some more widgets to retire" -- so the room comes from retirements they will name, not from arithmetic here.
